correctness.rationale: For n>=5, each of the n length-one and n length-two edges is distinct. Rayleigh-Ritz concavity makes the cyclic average of any feasible rate allocation at least as good. For class-constant a,b, Fourier diagonalization yields λ_k=a x_k+b x_k(4-x_k), x_k=4 sin²(pi k/n). Since b>=0, concavity in x puts the nonzero spectral minimum at x=mu or x=nu. The budget makes the two candidates affine in b; their slopes and unique intersection a=eta b give all three price regions, the entire equality families, and sharp endpoint formulas. eta=mu-r>0, 0<=r<q, so all cases exhaust t>0. Parity uses whether addition by two generates Z/n, and limits follow from sine asymptotics. The standalone checker, executed from the actual working path, reported VERIFY_OK with 23,760 uniform comparison tests, 972 nonuniform Jacobi spectral tests, 54 boundary tests, and 9 parity tests. Finite tests are corroboration only; no unproved infinite enumeration or algorithmic certification is claimed.

value.rationale: The priced square of a cycle is a natural communication architecture with competing nearest-neighbor and two-hop links; an explicit optimal continuous-time consensus rate is a motivated invariant. The theorem completely solves this all-n, all-positive-price design problem and all symmetric optimizer faces, rather than an arbitrary small instance or a rephrasing of a previously computed table. Exact thresholds r and q, an odd-only physically connected two-hop phase, and an asymptotically sharp gain 4/t directly answer which links should receive budget. The proof isolates a useful two-endpoint Fourier obstruction and avoids solving general SDPs. Reproducible computations alone are not treated as evidence of value. Limitations include nonuniform optimizer nonclassification and separate discrete-time objectives.
